rendering.ja: 『チェンバレンへ手紙を書くボリシェヴィキ』

«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену».note_for_reader: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, sent the USSR a hostile note in Feb. 1927; the Soviet press's slogan «Наш ответ Чемберлену» ('Our answer to Chamberlain') was the propaganda catchphrase of the year and is still proverbial. Ostap's title recasts Repin's famous canvas (in the same sentence) as that answer.
«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену».rationale: Kept denotation and the mock-solemn exhibition-catalogue register by translating the title literally and in each language echoing the established title of Repin's painting (Fisher's English wording, and the 写信 / 手紙を書く pattern of the standard zh/ja Repin titles) so the pastiche is visible; the 1927 topicality and the idiom «наш ответ Чемберлену» cannot be carried in a title and are given to a one-line note. Richardson's 'Answer Chamberlain' was set aside because it drops the literal 'writing a letter' link that the Russian sentence itself relies on.

улица имени товарища Губернского.finding: In chapter I of The Twelve Chairs (1928) this is the broad main street of the county town N where Vorobyaninov lives, lined by the coffin shops of the 'Nymph' bureau and Bezenchuk; it recurs later (Gos. No. 1 stuck at the corner of Staropanskaya Square and this street; Bender and Vorobyaninov come out onto it). The Odessky–Feldman commentary explains the joke: the typical main street of a provincial town was 'Gubernatorskaya' (Governor's Street), and the Soviet renaming 'named after Comrade Gubernsky' changes the sound but not the substance — a deadpan jab at the 1920s wave of renaming streets after party figures ('gubernsky' also means simply 'provincial'). A real ulitsa Gubernskogo exists in Novorossiysk (formerly Tsemesskaya; renamed for A. Yu. Gubernsky, shot by the Whites in 1918), and some scholars think Ilf and Petrov, who visited the city, borrowed it; the name is not a well-known person, so for the 1928 reader it read as a generic obscure local hero. Both English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) render it 'Comrade Gubernsky Street'; Zhang Peiwen's Chinese (People's Literature, 2004) has '名为古别伦斯基同志的大街'. No text of Egawa Takashi's Japanese translation is online, so the Japanese rendering is unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this term and was ignored.

rendering.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

улица имени товарища Губернского.note_for_reader: ‘Gubernsky’ sounds like ‘Governor’s/Provincial’: the town’s old Governor Street has been Soviet-renamed after an obscure ‘Comrade Gubernsky’ — a joke on 1920s street renaming.
улица имени товарища Губернского.rationale: Keeps denotation (a main street bearing a Soviet 'named after Comrade X' label) and the mock-solemn register by transliterating the name and keeping the 'Comrade' formula, as all existing EN and ZH translations do; gives up the Gubernatorskaya/Gubernsky pun, which the one-line note restores. ZH follows Zhang Peiwen's established 古别伦斯基 rather than a new transliteration; JA is a standard katakana form because Egawa's text could not be checked.

беспризорные.finding: Беспризорные (lit. 'unsupervised', 'uncared-for'; also беспризорники) were the orphaned and abandoned children of the World War, revolution, civil war and the 1921-22 Volga famine: estimates run to 4.5-7 million by 1921-22, falling to about 250,000 by 1926 after Dzerzhinsky's Children's Commission (Деткомиссия, 27 Jan 1921), mass round-ups (from April 1928) and orphanages and labour communes; a 1935 decree declared the phenomenon eliminated. They lived by begging, petty theft, peddling and prostitution, rode the rails, formed gangs with their own argot, and in cities slept in cellars and in the still-warm cauldrons used for boiling road asphalt, which is exactly the image in ch. XVI: 'Беспризорные сидели возле асфальтового чана и с наслаждением вдыхали запах кипящей смолы'. For a 1928 reader the word was a fixture of daily street life and of newspaper campaigns, not a euphemism: pitied and feared at once, a stock target of charity appeals (Ostap's fake 'Children's Aid' collection later in the book trades on this). English scholarship keeps the Russian word (besprizornye/besprizorniki) or says 'homeless children'; Richardson's 1961 translation uses 'waifs', en.wikipedia uses 'street children', 'waifs', 'urchins'. Chinese historical writing (e.g. the translation of Goldman's Women, the State and Revolution) uses 流浪儿童, while Chinese reviews of the novel say 流浪儿. Japanese coverage transliterates ベスプリゾルニキ with the gloss 家のない子どもたち, and Japanese writing on Makarenko's 1920s colonies uses 浮浪児.
беспризорные.note_for_reader: беспризорные: the millions of orphaned street children left by war, revolution and famine, a fixture of 1920s Soviet cities; they slept in cellars and in warm asphalt cauldrons.
беспризорные.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (unsupervised street children, not adults) and the period flavour: 'waifs' is Richardson's established word and carries the pity-plus-menace connotation, 流浪儿 is the wording Chinese readers of the novel already use, and 浮浪児 is the Japanese word for exactly this post-war phenomenon (Japan's own 1945 浮浪児), so it lands without explanation. Given up: the specifically Soviet scale and the state-campaign resonance of the word, which the one-line note restores; the Russian word itself is not carried, since a transliteration would mean nothing to this reader.

Клавдия Ивановна (Петухова).finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law in Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs: a pre-revolutionary provincial gentlewoman living with him in Stargorod, who on 15 April 1927 has a bad dream, suffers a stroke, and on her deathbed confesses to him and to Father Fyodor that she sewed her jewels into one of the twelve Gambs dining chairs. The chapter title 'Кончина мадам Петуховой' pairs the solemn 'кончина' with the pre-revolutionary, faintly bourgeois 'мадам', mock-obituary style, for a woman the narrator otherwise calls 'старуха' and 'теща' and whom her son-in-law openly dislikes. Existing renderings: John Richardson's English (1961, the standard one) uses 'Claudia Ivanovna', 'Madame Petukhov's Demise', 'the old woman', 'his mother-in-law'; Chinese: 张佩文 (人民文学 名著名译) uses 克拉芙季娅·伊万诺夫娜, chapter '别图霍娃夫人谢世', 岳母, 老太婆; 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺 2022) uses 佩图霍娃 ('佩图霍娃魂归地府'). Japanese: the only translation is 江川卓's 十二の椅子 (集英社 1966 / 筑摩 1969 / 世界ユーモア文庫 1977); no page found quoting its rendering of her name, so the Japanese form is by transliteration rule, not attested.

rendering.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜（彼图霍娃夫人）
rendering.ja: クラヴディヤ・イワーノヴナ（マダム・ペトゥホワ）

Клавдия Ивановна (Петухова).note_for_reader: 'Madame' in the chapter title is the narrator's mock-genteel, pre-revolutionary courtesy title for a woman the text otherwise calls 'the old woman' and 'his mother-in-law'.
Клавдия Ивановна (Петухова).rationale: Binds the name to three fixed forms that must stay distinct throughout: name-and-patronymic (Klavdia Ivanovna / 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜 / クラヴディヤ・イワーノヴナ) for the narrator's neutral voice, 'Madame Petukhova' / 彼图霍娃夫人 / マダム・ペトゥホワ only where the source has 'мадам Петухова' (the chapter title's mock obituary), and 'his mother-in-law' / 岳母 / 姑 (義母) plus 'the old woman' / 老太婆 / 老婆 for 'теща' and 'старуха'. Kept denotation and the ironic register; gave up Richardson's anglicised 'Claudia' and 'Petukhov' (feminine surname kept so the side-by-side reader can match the Russian) and, in Chinese, standardised 张佩文's 别图霍娃 / 徐昌翰's 佩图霍娃 to the modern standard 彼图霍娃; Japanese マダム rather than 夫人 keeps the faintly bourgeois, comic tint of 'мадам'.

«Прага», образцовая столовая МСПО.finding: «Прага» is the famous restaurant at Arbat 2, Moscow, made grand by the merchant Tararykin from the 1890s and, per Gilyarovsky, the best-appointed restaurant in the city. After nationalisation it reopened on 15 Oct 1924 as a public 'образцовая (образцово-показательная) столовая' of the Moscow consumer cooperative (sources name Моссельпром or МСПО; Mayakovsky's jingle ran «В столовой Моссельпрома — бывшая Прага»), keeping mirrors, flowers and an evening orchestra, i.e. a restaurant in all but name. МСПО = Московский союз потребительских обществ, the Moscow consumer co-op union (founded 1898; its national successor was Центросоюз). Shcheglov's commentary notes that in 1927 even Moscow's most representative restaurants were officially called столовые, so the joke is the officialese label 'model canteen' on a place where Vorobyaninov's bill comes to 9 r. 20 k. and Liza, who has never seen a 'large model restaurant', is dazzled. Richardson (1961) renders it 'the Prague Restaurant, the showpiece of the Moscow union of consumer societies'; Fisher's 2011 wording and the Chinese (张佩文, 徐昌翰, 白桦熊) and Japanese (江川卓) renderings were not accessible online. Japanese sources give Центросоюз as 消費者協同組合中央同盟 / ツェントロソユーズ; Wikidata's Chinese label is 苏联消费合作社.

rendering.en: the Prague, model canteen of the Moscow Consumer Co-op (MSPO)
rendering.zh: “布拉格”——莫斯科消费合作社联社（MSPO）的示范食堂
rendering.ja: モスクワ消費組合連合（MSPO）の模範食堂「プラーガ」

«Прага», образцовая столовая МСПО.note_for_reader: In NEP Moscow even the grandest restaurants were officially 'canteens' of a state or co-op body; the Prague, pre-1917 the city's most luxurious, was one such 'model canteen'.
«Прага», образцовая столовая МСПО.rationale: Keeps the denotation (the real Arbat restaurant, the co-op that ran it) and the ironic register of officialese 'model canteen / 示范食堂 / 模範食堂' set against a mirrored restaurant with a nine-ruble bill; gives up Richardson's smoother 'showpiece' and the expansion of МСПО beyond a short one-word-ish gloss, which the acronym in parentheses carries for cross-language matching.

Остап Бендер.finding: Ostap Bender is the fictional con-man protagonist of Ilf and Petrov's The Twelve Chairs (1928) and The Little Golden Calf (1931), self-styled Ostap-Suleyman-Berta-Maria-Bender-Bey, 'son of a Turkish subject' from Odessa; his surname is the Bessarabian town Bender/Bendery, and his epithet 'великий комбинатор' (the great schemer) became a Russian catchphrase. For a Russian reader of the 2010s the name is proverbial: 'Остап Бендер' or 'Бендер' means a charming, resourceful swindler who works '400 relatively honest ways' inside the letter of the law, and post-Soviet culture has half-rehabilitated him as an entrepreneur figure with statues in several cities. Every English translation (Richardson 1961, Fisher/Northwestern 2012) uses 'Ostap Bender'. Japanese editions (江川卓, Shueisha 1966/1969) and reference works (コトバンク) use オスタップ・ベンデル. Chinese usage is split: the older 徐昌翰 translation (春风文艺 1985, reissued 江苏凤凰文艺 2022) writes 奥斯塔普·本杰尔, while the newest translation (白桦熊, 上海译文 2021) and the CJK reference form use 奥斯塔普·本德尔; the latter matches the standard Xinhua transliteration of 'Бендер'. Note: the prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte is unrelated to this term and was ignored.

rendering.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

Остап Бендер.note_for_reader: Ostap Bender, the novel's 'great schemer', became a Russian byword for a charming swindler; 'Comrade Bender' is the standard Soviet form of address, and the newspaper notice's abbreviated 'т. Бендер' is kept abbreviated in English as 'Cde. Bender' (Chinese 本德尔同志 and Japanese ベンデル同志 have no printed abbreviation).
Остап Бендер.rationale: Denotation and register are kept exactly by binding the one transliteration each language's published translations already use (en unanimous; ja unanimous; zh the modern standard 本德尔 over the older 本杰尔); the connotation 'proverbial con man' cannot be carried by a name and is left to the narrative and a one-line note. For 'т. Бендер' use the abbreviated 'Cde. Bender' in English; Chinese and Japanese have no abbreviation for 同志, so keep 本德尔同志 / ベンデル同志 unabbreviated.

ГПУ.finding: ГПУ (Государственное политическое управление) was the Soviet secret police of the RSFSR, created on 6 February 1922 by VTsIK decree as the direct successor of the Cheka and placed inside the NKVD; on 15 November 1923 it became the all-Union ОГПУ under Sovnarkom. Despite the renaming, the short form 'ГПУ' stayed in the names of local organs and in everyday speech and literature (Bulgakov, Ilf and Petrov, Olesha, Mandelstam) through the 1920s-30s, so for a 1928 reader it simply meant 'the secret police', with the Cheka's menace still attached. In the novel the term is punchline material: Bender's 'Вам некуда торопиться. ГПУ к вам само придёт' (ch. 14, the 'Sword and Ploughshare' scene) became a proverb, and Russian sites still quote it as such. English coverage (Wikipedia, Fisher's translation apparatus) uses 'GPU' / 'State Political Directorate'; Chinese uses 国家政治保卫局 with the transliteration 格别乌; Japanese uses ゲーペーウー with 国家政治保安部 (or 国家政治局). The prompt's mention of 2013, Durov and VKontakte does not fit this term and was ignored; the research concerns the 1922-1928 institution.

rendering.en: the GPU (the secret police) — first occurrence; thereafter 'the GPU'
rendering.zh: 国家政治保卫局（格别乌，秘密警察）——首次出现；此后用“格别乌”
rendering.ja: ゲーペーウー（国家政治保安部、秘密警察）――初出のみ；以後は「ゲーペーウー」

ГПУ.note_for_reader: GPU: the Soviet secret police of the 1920s, successor to the Cheka and forerunner of the NKVD/KGB; renamed OGPU in 1923 but still called 'GPU' in speech.
ГПУ.rationale: Keeps denotation (an expanded gloss on first use in each language, using the established Wikipedia-level names) and register (the characters' flat, matter-of-fact acronym, which is what makes Bender's joke land), while giving up the automatic chill a 1928 reader felt at the letters; the one-line note supplies that instead of a footnote at every occurrence.

«Капля молока» и «Белый цветок».finding: Both are real pre-revolutionary charities, named here in Chapter XIX («Баллотировка по-европейски»), where the 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' conspirators hand out the offices of a restored old regime and «Елену Станиславовну выбрали попечительницей обществ «Капля молока» и «Белый цветок»». «Капля молока» (a calque of the French 'Goutte de lait', Fécamp 1891) was the name of infant-welfare stations that gave sterilised milk and doctor's consultations to poor mothers; the first Russian ones opened in St Petersburg and Odessa in 1901, and towns such as Arkhangelsk followed (1910). «Белый цветок» / «День белой ромашки» was the anti-tuberculosis flower day of the All-Russian League against Tuberculosis, first held 20 April 1911, in which society ladies and students sold paper daisies and the imperial family ran bazaars in Yalta; it stopped after 1917. For a 1928 reader the pair evoked the genteel, ladies'-committee philanthropy of the tsarist provincial town, so making the ex-mistress and fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna its 'patroness' is a joke about the conspirators' fantasy of restored respectability. Existing English, Chinese and Japanese renderings of this line (Richardson, Fisher, the Chinese and Egawa Japanese editions) could not be retrieved online; the literal society names are the only established form.

rendering.en: the 'Drop of Milk' and 'White Flower' charitable societies
rendering.ja: 「一滴のミルク」と「白い花」の両慈善協会

«Капля молока» и «Белый цветок».note_for_reader: Real tsarist-era charities: 'Drop of Milk' stations gave sterilised milk to poor infants; 'White Flower' was the anti-tuberculosis flower-day society (from 1911) patronised by society ladies and the imperial family.
«Капля молока» и «Белый цветок».rationale: Kept the denotation (literal, quoted society names, as in the source) and the mock-solemn register of the office list; added one word, 'charitable' (慈善/慈善), so the trilingual reader knows these are ladies' charities and gets the joke without a footnote, giving up the instant period colour a 1928 Russian reader had.

допр.finding: Допр (ДОПР) is a 1920s Soviet penal acronym; its expansion is itself contested: the Dictionary of the Language of Sovdepia and Russian Wikipedia give 'дом принудительных работ' / 'дом общественно-принудительных работ' (house of compulsory labour, one of the 'general places of confinement' of 1918–1922, transferred to the NKVD in 1923 and especially common in the Ukrainian SSR, e.g. Kharkiv and Stalino), while commentaries on the novel gloss it as 'дом предварительного заключения' (pre-trial detention house). In practice a допр held both remand prisoners and short-term convicts, so for a 1928 reader it meant simply 'the local jail', with a NEP-era flavour: Kislyarsky's 'допровская корзинка' in ch. 27 is the NEPman's ever-packed prison basket. In ch. VIII Ostap threatens Pasha Emilievich: 'Один мой знакомый тоже продавал государственную мебель. Теперь он пошел в монахи — сидит в допре' — 'went into a monastery' is a cell joke, and the punchline only lands if допр is plainly a jail. Anne O. Fisher's 2011 translation (Northwestern) renders it 'He's doing time in the lockup' (p. 100) and uses 'lockup' again for Kislyarsky's basket (p. 411); Richardson's 1961 abridgement has no trace of the line (search-within finds no monk/lockup passage there) and uses 'jail' for the basket chapter. No published Chinese or Japanese rendering of this line could be located online.
допр.rationale: Keeps denotation (a jail, not a labour camp) and the offhand colloquial register so the 'became a monk' joke stays plain; gives up the period acronym and its specifically Soviet/Ukrainian institutional connotation. 'The lockup' is Fisher's established English; 看守所 and 拘置所 are the everyday modern words for a pre-trial jail in Chinese and Japanese, instantly clear without a note.

«На заре ты ее не буди».finding: First line and title of Afanasy Fet's 1842 poem, set the same year by Alexander Varlamov as a drawing-room romance (first sung by the tenor Bantyshev); by 1850 the critic Apollon Grigoriev already called it 'almost a folk song', and it remained a standard of the Russian romance repertoire (Lemeshev, Viktoria Ivanova, Pogudin) into the 2010s, so a Russian reader of 2013 heard it instantly as a sentimental old song. In Chapter XIV Ostap uses it as mock-tender cover for stealing the chair from his sleeping bride, the widow Gritsatsueva, before leaving the note 'Going to Novokhopersk with a report. Don't wait for me at dinner. Your Suslik.' The joke is the gap between the languid parlour lyric and the burglary it excuses. The standard English translation (John Richardson, 1961) renders it as the bare quotation 'Don't wake her at dawn!' with no attribution; the romance itself is sold in English as 'Do not wake her at dawn'. No established Chinese or Japanese title for the poem or romance surfaced in search (a Japanese art-song index lists the poem only under an ad-hoc gloss), and no rendering from the Chinese (费明君, 安郁琛/钟鼎, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓) translations of the novel could be retrieved.

rendering.zh: 《黎明时莫将她唤醒》（费特的浪漫曲）
rendering.ja: 「暁に彼女を起こすな」（フェートのロマンス）

«На заре ты ее не буди».note_for_reader: Opening line of Fet's 1842 poem, set by Varlamov as one of the best-known Russian drawing-room romances.
«На заре ты ее не буди».rationale: Keeps the denotation and the quotation-marking (quotes plus a two-word source tag, so the reader knows Ostap is singing, not confessing) and the mock-tender register in all three languages; gives up the instant recognition a Russian reader had, which the one-line note restores, and in zh/ja gives up an established title because none exists to prefer.

концессионеры / компаньоны.finding: In the Russian text (az.lib.ru) 'концессия' and 'концессионеры' occur about 68 times and 'компаньоны' about 19: Ostap frames the treasure hunt as a 'концессия' from the first bargaining scene ('как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов'), and the narrator then mock-solemnly calls the pair 'концессионеры', Ostap 'главный концессионер' / 'технический директор' and Vorobyaninov 'директор-учредитель концессии', alternating with the plainer 'компаньоны'. A концессия in 1920s usage was the NEP-specific licence under which a foreign firm (Lena Goldfields, Harriman's manganese, Hammer's Alapayevsk asbestos, Krupp's Manych farm) was allowed to run a state-owned enterprise for profit, per the Sovnarkom decree of 23 Nov 1920; they were headline news and a byword for capitalist money-making in Soviet Russia until the Main Concessions Committee was wound up around 1930. So the joke is that two private jewel-hunters style themselves a quasi-official foreign-capital enterprise, complete with percentages and 'соцстрах'. Both published English versions keep it: John Richardson (1971, lib.ru) uses 'concessionaires' ~65 times and 'partners' for компаньоны, and Anne O. Fisher (Northwestern UP, 2011) also writes 'the concessionaires'. For Chinese, the established historiographic term for NEP concessions is 租让制/租让企业 (Lenin's 1921 租让 principles), not 特许经营 (which now reads as franchising); for Japanese, Soviet-era concessions are conventionally 利権 (e.g. 北樺太石油利権) or コンセッション. I could not retrieve the actual in-text renderings of the Chinese (徐昌翰 1985, 张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) translations; those are inferred from the historical terminology, not verified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'a Russian reader around 2013' does not match this 1928 novel and was ignored.

rendering.ja: 利権者たち / 共同経営者たち

концессионеры / компаньоны.note_for_reader: A 'concession' (концессия) was the NEP-era licence letting a foreign firm run a Soviet state enterprise for profit; Ostap grandly styles the two-man jewel hunt as one, so the narrator calls the pair 'concessionaires'.
концессионеры / компаньоны.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a NEP concession, via the period term in each language: concession / 租让 / 利権) and the mock-official register, with a plain business word for компаньоны so the two names stay distinct; gives up the automatic 1928 recognition that the joke was topical, which the one-line note supplies. 特许经营者 and 利権屋 were rejected: the first shifts to modern franchising, the second adds a slangy 'profiteer' sneer the deadpan narrator does not have.

толстовка.finding: In the novel (ch. XXI 'Экзекуция', auction scene) the word is a garment: the auctioneer's beard falls onto 'толстовку русского коверкота'. A толстовка of the 1910s–20s is a long, loose men's blouse worn outside the trousers, usually belted, with dense gathers or pleats, a standing collar, buttoned front and chest pockets — a cross between a soldier's гимнастёрка and a peasant shirt, named after the loose shirt in which the aged Tolstoy was endlessly photographed; the word itself entered Russian only in the late 1910s and Tolstoy never used it. In the early Soviet years it was popular for its 'democratic', anti-bourgeois look (as opposed to a suit) among office workers, intellectuals, writers and artists, and by 1930 it had gone out of fashion except among artists; in 1928 it read as the standard, slightly earnest uniform of a Soviet служащий, so a bearded auctioneer in loud checked trousers plus a covert-cloth толстовка is a mildly absurd mix. The modern sense 'sweatshirt/hoodie' dates only from the 1980s–90s and must not leak in. Existing English coverage (Wikipedia, the Master and Margarita annotations, the standard shop name) uses 'Tolstoy blouse' / 'Tolstoy shirt'; Japanese sources either transliterate トルストフカ or explain it via ルバシカ and give no fixed descriptive term; Chinese sources use 托尔斯泰衬衫 for the Tolstoy-style shirt. I could not retrieve the exact sentence in the Richardson or Fisher English translations, so their choice is unverified. (The brief's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term.)
толстовка.note_for_reader: Tolstovka: the loose, belted, pleated over-shirt Tolstoy wore; in the 1920s the plain 'democratic' dress of Soviet clerks and intellectuals — not today's sweatshirt.
толстовка.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a period garment named for Tolstoy) and the neutral register, and a reader who knows Tolstoy's portraits gets the image; what is given up is the 1928 connotation of a bland Soviet-office uniform, which the one-line note restores. 'Blouse' rather than 'shirt' in English signals the loose belted cut; zh and ja follow the only existing usages found and stay transparent for the target reader.

загс.finding: ЗАГС is the acronym of 'запись актов гражданского состояния' (registration of acts of civil status): the local Soviet office that registers births, marriages, divorces and deaths. It was created by the Sovnarkom decree of 18 December 1917 on civil marriage and the 1918 code, which took these functions away from the church's parish 'metric books' and made only state registration legally valid, so by 1928 the word was everyday, lower-case Russian (ru.wikipedia writes 'загс' as a common noun; 'пойти в загс' still means 'to get married'). In chapter 1 the original reads 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков' and the joke turns on the 'толстые книги' in which everything born or married that day is written down: the ex-marshal of the nobility now keeps the secular successor of the parish register in a provincial town. Richardson's 1961 English translation renders it simply 'registry office' (no acronym); Fisher's 2011 version could not be checked online. Japanese dictionaries give the standard gloss 戸籍登録課, reading ザークス (kotobank Russian-Japanese dictionary), and ja.wikipedia lists ЗАГС as 戸籍登録機関; a Chinese ebook translation found online domesticates it as 民政局 (a PRC civil-affairs bureau), which is anachronistic. The prompt's mention of 'Durov and VKontakte around 2013' does not apply to this term and was ignored.
загс.note_for_reader: ZAGS: Soviet acronym for the office of 'civil-status acts', which in 1917–18 replaced church parish registers as the only legal record of births, marriages and deaths.
загс.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state office for births, marriages, deaths) and carry the acronym once so later bare 'ZAGS'/'ザークス' and the thick-ledger joke land; the Japanese uses the dictionary-standard 戸籍登録 and reading ザークス rather than 登記/ザーグス, and the Chinese uses 民事登记 instead of 户籍登记 because 户籍 would make a PRC reader think of hukou residence registration. Given up: the flat bureaucratic sound of a Soviet acronym as an ordinary word, which no target language reproduces without a gloss.

предводитель (дворянства).finding: Предводитель дворянства was the elected head of the nobility of a district (уезд) or province (губерния), instituted by Catherine II's 1785 Charter to the Nobility and abolished in 1917: chosen by the noble assembly for a three-year term, unpaid, confirmed by the governor (district) or the emperor (province), chairing the zemstvo assembly, school and conscription boards, so that the district marshal was the de facto head of his district. To a 1928 or 2013 Russian reader it is the quintessential 'former person' title: a gentry grandee of the old regime, now an ex-. In the novel Ostap's habitual vocative is the bare 'предводитель' ('Вам, предводитель, пора уже лечиться электричеством'; 'а вы, предводитель, не жмите девочку'), he mocks 'для предводителя дворянства у вас слишком мелкие масштабы', and at the auction escalates to 'Не бойтесь, гофмаршал!'; I could not find the exact wording 'Молитесь, предводитель' on Wikisource, where the auction line reads 'Молитесь на меня, молитесь!'. English coverage (Richardson 1961, Wikipedia) uniformly uses 'marshal of the nobility'; Japanese uses 貴族団長 (ja.wikipedia article; Anna Karenina character lists give 県貴族団長; Japanese summaries of the novel call Vorobyaninov 元貴族団長); Chinese editions of the novel (徐昌翰, 后浪 2022 description) and the People's Literature Anna Karenina use 首席贵族 / 省首席贵族, as does Chinese historiography (张宗华), while 贵族长 is rarer. I could not verify how Richardson or Fisher render the bare vocative.

предводитель (дворянства).note_for_reader: Marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства): the elected head of a district's gentry under the tsars, an unpaid but powerful local dignitary; abolished in 1917. Ostap's 'Marshal' is a jeer at Vorobyaninov's lost rank.
предводитель (дворянства).rationale: Kept the established denotation in all three languages (marshal of the nobility / 首席贵族 / 貴族団長) and a one-word vocative in each (Marshal / 首席 / 団長) whose slightly wrong secondary sense (military marshal, CEO-style 'chief', troupe leader) reproduces Ostap's mock-solemn deflation; gave up the transparency of 'leader of the nobility' and, in Chinese, the shorter but less attested 贵族长.

милиционер.finding: A милиционер is a rank-and-file member of the милиция, the ordinary uniformed police of Soviet Russia. The name comes from a Provisional Government decree of 17 April 1917 and was reaffirmed by the Bolsheviks on 10 November 1917 as the 'Workers' and Peasants' Militia', deliberately avoiding the tsarist word полиция, which connoted autocratic repression; the intended association was with popular self-organisation rather than a professional state force. By 1928 the word was fully lexicalised and neutral: in the novel a милиционер is simply the man at the crossroads with a traffic baton, a cop to be edged past by an ice-cream seller or a con man, with no overtone of armed irregulars. Russia only renamed the force полиция on 1 March 2011, so for every Russian reader before then милиционер was the plain everyday word for policeman. In English, the 1961 Richardson translation uses 'militiaman' throughout (e.g. the ice-cream seller who 'squinted timorously at the militiaman ... regulating the traffic'); English Wikipedia notes the institution is usually left as 'militsiya' or glossed 'police'. Japanese coverage renders the institution ミリツィヤ（民警） and Chinese coverage 苏联民警 (alongside 苏联民兵), so 民警 is the established rendering in both. I could not verify Anne Fisher's (2011) choice directly.
милиционер.note_for_reader: Soviet police were called the 'militia' (милиция) from 1917 to 2011 to mark a break with the tsarist 'police'; a милиционер is an ordinary uniformed policeman, not an irregular.
милиционер.rationale: For English I keep denotation and the neutral everyday register at the cost of the Soviet-specific connotation, since 'militiaman' (Richardson's choice) suggests armed irregulars to a non-specialist; one note at first occurrence carries the lost nuance. For Chinese and Japanese 民警 keeps all three: it is the established term for the Soviet militsiya in both languages and reads as an ordinary neighbourhood policeman (the PRC's own 人民警察 are also called 民警), so no note is needed there.

Заседание продолжается!.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring catchphrase (first in ch. 6, then chs. 12, 21, 30, 40 etc.), always in the same courtroom-chairman idiom as his 'Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели!': Ostap casts himself as presiding judge and Vorobyaninov as the jury, so in ch. 21 'Заседание продолжается! Слышите? Вы! Присяжный заседатель!' turns 'juryman' into a jeer at his useless partner. Dushenko's Большой словарь цитат and dslov.ru trace the formula to Charles Dupuy, president of the French Chamber of Deputies, who after Vaillant's bomb on 9 Dec 1893 said 'Messieurs, la séance continue!'; by 1928 it was a stock phrase of unflappable officialdom that Ilf and Petrov hand to a con man. In Russian it became a proverb meaning 'the business goes on, nothing has stopped us' and is listed in every dictionary of крылатые слова. Established renderings: John Richardson's English (lib.ru, cited by Wikipedia) uses 'The hearing is continued' throughout and 'Hey you, member of the jury?' for the ch. 21 insult; the 2022 Shanghai Translation edition (tr. 白桦熊) is marketed with the catchphrase as '庭审继续进行！' alongside '陪审员先生们'; no Japanese wording from Egawa Taku's 1966/1969 translation could be verified online.
Заседание продолжается!.note_for_reader: Ostap's catchphrase apes a presiding judge or chairman (famously Charles Dupuy's 'Messieurs, la séance continue!' after the 1893 bomb in the French Chamber); he addresses his partner as the jury, so 'juryman' here is a taunt.
Заседание продолжается!.rationale: All three keep the courtroom frame so the phrase can sit beside 'gentlemen of the jury / 陪审员先生们 / 陪審員諸君' and the 'juryman' insult; en and zh bind the published renderings (Richardson; Shanghai Translation 2022) rather than the flatter 'session/meeting continues', which loses the jury pairing. The Dupuy allusion and the proverb status are given up (a one-line note carries them); ja is a defensible novel wording since Egawa's text could not be checked.

«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по.term: «Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по Репину: «Запорожцы пишут письмо султану»)
«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по.finding: In the Stargorod chapters Bender considers offering the local children's commission an 'as yet unpainted but brilliantly conceived' picture, hoping for some 400 rubles, and worries only that it would be technically hard to show Kalinin in a papakha and white burka and Chicherin bare to the waist. The model is Repin's 'Запорожцы' (1880–91, Russian Museum), popularly called 'Запорожцы пишут письмо турецкому султану'; the standard English title is 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks', with 'Cossacks Writing a Letter to the Turkish Sultan' as an accepted alternate; ja: 『トルコのスルタンへ手紙を書くザポロージャ・コサック』; zh: 《扎波罗热哥萨克致土耳其苏丹的回信》 / 《扎波罗热人写信给土耳其苏丹》 (older art books: 《查波罗什人写信给苏丹王》). Chamberlain is Sir Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, whose note of 23 Feb 1927 demanded the USSR stop anti-British propaganda and aid to the Chinese revolution; Pravda's 'Our reply to Chamberlain!' became the slogan of the year, even naming an Osoaviakhim air-fleet fund. The joke is doubly topical: a 1923 'Krasny Perets' cartoon had already posed Bolshevik leaders (including Kalinin and Chicherin) as Repin's Cossacks writing to Lord Curzon, and 'Krokodil' ran 'Workers Write a Reply to Chamberlain' in 1927, so a 1928 reader saw Bender plagiarising a well-worn agitprop cliché to milk a state committee. The English, Chinese and Japanese translations of the novel do not appear to have a canonical rendering online; the Repin title in each language is the fixed point.

«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по.note_for_reader: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary, sent Moscow an ultimatum-like note in Feb 1927; 'Our reply to Chamberlain!' was the Soviet slogan of the year, and cartoons had already recast Repin's laughing Cossacks as Bolshevik leaders (Kalinin, the head of state; Chicherin, the foreign commissar).
«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» (по.rationale: Denotation and the mock-solemn register are kept by mirroring the novel's own descriptive title of the Repin picture in each language's established form; the connotation that Bender is recycling a stale agitprop cliché of 1927 cannot survive without the note, which carries it.

великий комбинатор.finding: Ilf and Petrov's fixed narratorial epithet for Ostap Bender in Двенадцать стульев (1928; it titles chapter 5) and Золотой телёнок (1931; it titles chapter 1). 'Комбинатор' in 1920s usage meant a man of 'комбинации' — clever, not-quite-honest deals — and 'великий' gives it mock-epic solemnity; Russian dictionaries define the phrase as 'ловкий пройдоха, добивающийся успеха путём сложных операций, уловок, мошенничества' and note it became a proverbial catchphrase, ironic or disapproving, for any slick schemer. English translators split: Richardson (1961, the standard edition) uses 'the smooth operator' (chapter 5 title), Malamuth's Golden Calf 'the great schemer', Fisher (2009/2011) 'the grand strategist', while Wikipedia glosses it 'The Great Combinator / The Great Schemer'. Chinese editions likewise vary: 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) 伟大谋士, 白桦熊 (上海译文 2022) 了不起的幕僚, with 伟大的谋略家 common in Chinese commentary. No fixed Japanese epithet was found in coverage of the 江川卓 (1966/1969) or 上田進 (1957) translations; reviews describe Bender as 大詐欺師 or 策士. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this term; the 1928 novel context was used.
великий комбинатор.note_for_reader: Великий комбинатор, 'the Grand Schemer': the narrator's mock-heroic title for Bender, now a Russian byword for a charming con man.
великий комбинатор.rationale: All three keep the mock-solemn 'great/grand + agent noun' shape so the epithet is recognisable across the parallel columns and stays fixed; 'Grand Schemer' is a near-variant of the established Malamuth/Wikipedia 'great schemer' with Fisher's 'grand', and 谋略家/策士 both carry 'strategist' with a shady undertone. Given up: Richardson's idiomatic but un-grand 'smooth operator', the 1920s flavour of 'комбинация', and the phrase's proverbial afterlife, which no target reader can feel without the note.

финагент.finding: Финагент is the Soviet-era clipped compound 'финансовый агент' (Ushakov marks it 'нов.'), the lowest rung of the Narkomfin district tax staff: the 1925 Regulation on external tax supervision set out фининспектор, their assistants, and финагенты, and assigned the actual collection of payments (взимание платежей) to the agents, while inspectors assessed income. So a финагент is the man who physically calls on shopkeepers and mattress-owners to take the money, not an auditor or a broker. In chapter XVII ('Уважайте матрацы, граждане!') Ilf and Petrov use him as a stock figure of NEP everyday life who arrives 'в целях фискальных' and, having gathered the tax like a bee gathering the spring nectar-flow, 'с радостным гулом улетает в свой участковый улей'. For a 1928 reader the word carried mild dread and ridicule (cf. Mayakovsky's fininspektor): the petty state functionary who materialises as soon as you own anything. Richardson's 1961 English (the only full text online) renders the same passage 'Having collected his tax like a bumblebee gathering spring honey, the tax collector flies away with a joyful hum to his district hive', and 'income-tax collector' in the preceding sentence and in chapter III. I could not locate the Chinese (张佩文 / 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) wording of this sentence online; the zh/ja choices below are therefore mine.
финагент.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a low-level official who comes to collect, which is what the bee-and-hive image needs) and the established English precedent; 'tax collector' / 收税员 / 徴税吏 deliberately rank him below the proposed 'inspector' / 稽查员 / 官, which is closer to fact. What is given up is the Soviet acronym flavour of фин-, which no target language can carry without a note, and which the mock-solemn sentence supplies anyway.

«Сказка любви дорогой».finding: Not a song title in itself but a line from the refrain of the 1915 drawing-room romance «Молчи, грусть, молчи» (words Anatoly D'Aktil/Frenkel, music Grigory Berezovsky; the commentary in the Odessky–Feldman-annotated text credits B. Grodzky): «Молчи, грусть, молчи, / Не тронь старых ран, / Сказки любви дорогой / Не вернуть никогда, никогда». «дорогой» is 'dear, precious', not 'expensive'. The same two lines became the titles of Pyotr Chardynin's 1918 two-part melodrama starring Vera Kholodnaya, whose part two was released as «Сказка любви дорогой»; the annotators say the novel may allude to either the romance or the film. In the chapter at the Furniture Museum, Ippolit Matveevich, aged 52, exchanges names with Liza Kalachova and the line pops into his head as he peers at her «простенькое лицо» — for a 1928 reader it was instantly recognisable pre-war salon kitsch, the mental soundtrack of a fossil, and the deadpan narration undercuts it at once with his grabbing her hand. Richardson's English (1961) renders it 'A tale of true love'; Fisher's 2011 rendering could not be checked online. The film is 'Be Silent, My Sorrow, Be Silent' in English Wikipedia and 「黙れ、わが悲しみ、黙れ」 in Japanese Wikipedia; no Chinese or Japanese rendering of the second-part title or of the refrain line was found.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ヴェーラ・ホロドナヤ
«Сказка любви дорогой».note_for_reader: A line from the refrain of the 1915 salon romance 'Hush, my sorrow, hush' (Молчи, грусть, молчи), also the title of a 1918 Vera Kholodnaya melodrama — pre-revolutionary sentimental kitsch surfacing in Vorobyaninov's head.
«Сказка любви дорогой».rationale: All three keep the denotation (a tale of dear/precious love) and the kitsch register of a sentimental song title in quotation marks: the inverted 'Love So Dear', the Chinese 爱情童话 cliché, and the archaic Japanese いとしき all signal old-fashioned sentimentality; what is given up is the recognition effect — the target reader cannot hear the melody or the Kholodnaya film — which the one-line note supplies.
